🤖 AGI by spring 2027? AI is already helping build its successor.

OpenAI says its AI is helping develop the next generation of models — handling research tasks that would take a skilled researcher several days, with humans supervising.

That could change the pace of progress. GPT-6 Astra helps researchers build a stronger model. Its successor takes on harder research problems and helps develop the generation after that.

The better AI gets at research, the faster this cycle could become.

OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, says internal results give him reason to expect progress toward this kind of self-improvement. His concern: safety checks and human oversight may struggle to keep up.

Spring 2027 is still a bet. Faster research tasks don’t automatically produce faster breakthroughs: experiments need computing power, and results need verification.

But Astra’s contribution to AGI may extend beyond anything it says in a chat. It could be helping researchers build the model that gets us closer.

💬 When do you expect AGI: 2027, 2030, or much later?

🤖 OpenAI says its AI has solved the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, a mathematical question unresolved for roughly 90 years.

An internal model, described as significantly more capable than GPT-6 Astra, powered a group of around 10,000 concurrent agents.

The agents reached the solution after just 88 hours. Lean formalization and verification took another 17 hours via GPT-6 Astra.

The reported result: smooth three-dimensional fluid motion can develop a singularity in finite time under a smooth external force, while total energy remains finite.

OpenAI is sharing the proof and its Lean formalization. 130 billion output tokens went into the Navier–Stokes effort alone. The internal model is still training.

⚡️An AI-designed drug may have made people biologically younger

Rentosertib just delivered a fascinating result: after 12 weeks of treatment, six different biological-age clocks all estimated patients to be roughly 3–4 years younger.

The six clocks came from independent groups, used different features and weren’t trained on the same data. Two measure mortality risk, while four track chronological age, yet they still moved in the same direction.

• 54 statistical tests. 21 were significant.
• By chance, only about 0.15 would be expected.

Nobel laureate Michael Levitt says the agreement between the clocks is what caught his attention, while stressing that the study cannot yet prove slower aging, since treating a lung condition could itself change the biomarkers.

The next test is Healthy volunteers. If those results hold, things get very interesting.

The first experiment is done. Now the race is to see whether AI can actually help us turn back the biological clock.

Source.

❗️OpenAI used $15 MILLION in tokens to tackle this 90-year-old mathematical mystery.

The Navier–Stokes equations describe how fluids move, from water swirling in a glass to air flowing over a wing. 

The mystery is whether a smooth 3D flow can remain stable forever, or tighten into a singularity where velocity becomes infinite in finite time.

OpenAI deployed 10,000 coordinating AI agents, which would cost an everyday user $15M in tokens, paired with a next-generation model. The system first solved a simpler version before producing a full result in just 88 hours.

The proposed solution identifies a vortex that spirals inward and stretches until the flow breaks down, while total energy remains finite.

The proof was then formally verified in Lean, allowing a computer to check every logical step.

The problem carries a $1 MILLION Clay Mathematics Institute prize, which OpenAI says it will not accept.

🔥 Google DeepMind just mapped 9 billion DNA variants

We’re moving from simply reading the human genome to using AI to predict what happens when we change it. 

DeepMind’s AlphaGenome can analyze up to 1 million DNA base pairs and predict how genetic variants affect gene expression, RNA splicing, chromatin and more.

Around 98% of human DNA doesn’t directly code for proteins, yet changes in these regions can still influence disease.

AlphaGenome can sift through billions of variants and flag the ones most likely to matter.

Early research found 22% more non-coding genetic associations in UK Biobank data.

If this keeps accelerating, AI could turn the genome from a massive instruction manual into something we can predict, simulate and eventually engineer. 

The future of medicine might be less about treating disease… and more about predicting it before it starts.

🐋 DeepSeek just made its AI architecture much cheaper

⚡️ GPT-6 Astra just solved a problem medical students have been facing for decades

Medical students have been working around the same three problems for decades. Someone talked to them, identified all three, and built a service with Astra that solves them in one tool.

The problems are structural. Flat anatomical diagrams strip depth out of organs entirely. CT cross-sections don't connect naturally to the overview diagrams students spend years memorizing. And reading a scan requires holding three mental models simultaneously - patient orientation, cross-section direction, and how every organ shape shifts through each layer.

Astra built a service that handles all three in one place. Not a better textbook. A spatial tool that connects the diagram, the CT view, and the 3D relationship together.

Medical education hasn't changed its core format in over a century. This might be the first tool designed around how anatomy is actually understood - not just displayed.

🤖 Claude Reached Real Systems in Tests

Anthropic reviewed 4 cases where Claude gained internet access during cyber tests and attacked real third-party systems. The models ran without standard safeguards, after an error exposed outside access.

Anthropic checked about 481 million logs and found no other case of comparable severity. New models perform better. METR will conduct an independent incident review.

❗️Dario Amodei just published a new essay on the future of AI

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has published a new essay, “We Must Pace the Frontier,” arguing that the AI industry may need to deliberately slow the pace of frontier development before AI progress starts moving faster than our ability to control it.

His concern is that AI is increasingly being used to accelerate AI research itself. Once that feedback loop becomes powerful enough, capability gains could compound rapidly, leaving safety research struggling to keep up.

Amodei isn’t calling for an AI pause or a halt to development. Instead, he argues for “pacing” the frontier, creating checkpoints where increasingly capable AI systems have to meet specific safety requirements before development continues.

His proposals include independent third-party evaluators with deep access to frontier labs, coordination between democratic governments, and eventually international agreements around the most powerful AI systems.
